source.title: A single impurity in an ideal atomic Fermi gas: current understanding and some open problems

accepted.question_text: For a single spinless impurity of mass M immersed in a zero-temperature 3D polarized atomic Fermi gas of background atoms of mass m with tunable s-wave impurity-background scattering length a, determine whether the dressed single-impurity branch called the polaron and the dressed branch connected to the impurity-background dimer called the dimeron are genuinely distinct energy branches, or instead the same branch connected continuously across the polaron-to-dimeron transition near k_F a ~ 1. In particular, determine whether the ground-state wave function is continuous across that transition and, in the small-m/M regime where the transition becomes continuous for a fixed impurity, whether the transition as a function of the mass ratio m/M is smooth at the critical 1/k_F a_c or remains discontinuous.

evidence.quote: We raise a few unsolved problems: whether the polaron and dimeron are really separate branches

Edwards [29] has raised the question of whether the polaron and dimeron energy branches are really separate or one and the same (i.e. is the groundstate wave function continuous across the polaron-to-dimeron transition at kFa ∼ 1?).
Is there a more definitive theoretical argument? Barring that, can we at least make a plausibility argument?
Is this a smooth transition at the critical 1/kF ac as a function of m/M: ... with α,β > 0? Or does it happen discontinuously?

accepted.question_text: In the same single-impurity Fermi-gas system, and assuming m/M < 13.384 so that Efimov states have not yet appeared, determine whether there exist stable non-Efimovian bound states in vacuum larger than the already known dimer, trimer, and tetramer, such as pentamers, hexamers, or still larger impurity-plus-identical-fermion clusters, for given values of the mass ratio m/M and positive scattering length a > 0.

evidence.quote: We raise a few unsolved problems: ... what other few-body states might exist
Assuming that m/M < 13.384 is the lower limit for the appearance of Efimov states, can there be other larger, stable, non-Efimovian few-body states (pentamers, hexamers and so on) below that limit?
These have not been investigated to our knowledge since they are computationally unwieldy.

accepted.question_text: For a system consisting of a single impurity interacting with identical fermions through the wide-resonance Hamiltonian, prove or disprove that, for fixed mass ratio m/M and scattering length a, there is an upper limit on the number of fermions that can belong to a stable non-Efimovian bound state with that impurity, either in vacuum or with a Fermi sea present.

evidence.quote: Perhaps, from the theoretical point of view, it is more interesting to ask the question: could we prove the existence of an upper limit (with Fermi sea present or in vacuum) to the number of fermions in a non-Efimovian bound state with a single impurity for given m/M, a?
However, Pauli blocking would then increase their kinetic energy and the problem would get worse for larger number of fermions.

accepted.question_text: Given the many-body wave function of a single impurity in a Fermi gas expanded in sectors with increasing numbers of particle-hole pairs, determine the asymptotic form of the large-s tail of that wave function, where s is the number of particle-hole pairs. In particular, characterize the regime of very large s that controls the coherence properties of the impurity and decide whether that asymptotic tail can be described analytically using an effectively noninteracting gas of particles and holes that each scatter only from the impurity.

evidence.quote: We raise a few unsolved problems: ... the nature of the groundstate for large numbers of particle-hole pairs
What is the asymptotic wave function for large particle-hole numbers?
So far there has been no study of the “tail” of the wave function - the asymptotic form for large number s of particle-hole pairs.
The theoretical interest here is the connection with the problem of the coherence of the impurity in a Fermi gas.

accepted.question_text: Explain why the Chevy ansatz, obtained by truncating the impurity wave-function expansion to a single particle-hole pair, remains extremely accurate even for large scattering length where strong particle-hole correlations might be expected. Determine whether the particle-hole-pair expansion has a hidden small parameter, identify when that expansion fails if it does fail, and quantify how the truncation error in observables such as the energy and quasiparticle residue depends on the truncation order, the mass ratio m/M, and the interaction parameter 1/k_F a.

evidence.quote: We raise a few unsolved problems: ... why is the polaron ansatz so good.
Why is the Chevy ansatz so good?

The Chevy ansatz seems to be extremely good even for large scattering length where we would expect strong particle-hole correlations, particularly for the energy and Z [28]. Why? Does the particle-hole pair expansion of the wave function have a hidden small parameter? And when does it fail (if ever)?
We would like to have a more quantitative control of the error when truncating the expansion at a certain order.

Are these two effects enough to show that terms with larger number of particle-hole pairs have smaller contributions and can we estimate the error in various quantities when truncating to a certain order in particle-hole pair number? Also, how would this error vary with m/M and 1/kFa?

accepted.question_text: When the effective mass M* of the impurity quasiparticle is extracted by minimizing a truncated variational trial state at small but nonzero momentum p and fitting E_p = E_0 + p^2/(2M*), determine whether this variational procedure is mathematically well defined and whether it really computes the real part of the complex excitation energy of the long-lived dressed impurity state.

evidence.quote: This raises the question of whether the variational method is a well defined procedure for finding the effective mass.
As far as we know it has not been shown that this corresponds to calculating the real part of the complex excitation energy discussed above.

accepted.question_text: For composite dressed quasiparticles in this impurity problem, including the dimeron, trimeron, and tetrameron, determine whether there is a stronger general lower bound on the effective mass than positivity alone, namely whether dressing always increases the mass so that M*_b / M_b >= 1, where M_b is the bare mass of the corresponding composite bound state and M*_b is its effective mass in the Fermi gas.

evidence.quote: Is there a better bound for dimerons, trimerons and tetramerons?
We conjecture that the dressing always increases the mass, even for composite particles: M∗ b /Mb ≥ 1?
All calculations of the effective mass of the dimeron so far are consistent with this simple generalisation [5, 20].
